The official training partition is split by individual record (seeded, stratified 70/15/15) into initial-training, validation, and adaptation parts, with no grouping by capture session, source, or attack campaign. The dataset also has known overlap and imbalance issues [15]
Related records could occur in more than one of these parts, which is a risk of dependence and of optimistic results and not demonstrated leakage. The official test partition was not split this way
Eleven normalized features are perturbed within a fixed L∞ bound, with no packet reconstruction or protocol checks [4], [23], [24]

Neither attack-induced ASR nor the post-attack benign rate shows that the perturbed flows could occur in real traffic. Most perturbed flows break the tcprtt and rate relations, and perturbed non-TCP flows receive TCP timing values (Section 5.10)
Evasion labels come from dataset ground truth, as an idealized oracle
Real analyst delay, error, and workload are not measured
Unmatched budgets in the main comparison

The static arm uses 500 pre-built examples and the incremental arms use about 21 to 111 successful-evasion labels. The extension matched the number and source-flow set of attack attempts, not the perturbed vectors, and one arm also matched optimizer steps and exposure

Main-comparison differences cannot be attributed to scheduling. In the extension, the matched arms' order followed training structure and exposure (Section 5.8). The matched incremental schedule trains on all attempts, so it is not the successful-evasion policy of arms C to E, and other matching rules were not tested
Each round attacks the current model afresh, with no attacker that learns across rounds and no defense-aware attack
Results do not cover an adaptive adversary
In the decision-only evaluation of the main comparison, the static arm is trained on FGSM-like examples. The extension adds B-dec, trained on decision-only examples
B-dec had higher observed attack-induced ASR than the cross-attack static arm, so using the threat-model-matched baseline would not have lowered the static arm's observed ASR in that setting
The main comparison used one configuration per policy. The extension varied update epochs, learning rate, and memory size one at a time for arms C, M1, M1-e10, and M2, in the FGSM-like setting only

In the FGSM-like setting, M2 had lower observed ASR than M1 and higher observed ASR than M1-e10 in most seeds in all seven configurations (Section 5.9). The BIM-like and decision-only settings, M1-seq, other policies, and combinations of settings were not varied
The cohort contains only flows the initial model detected at the fixed threshold, and updates use the fixed threshold while the primary evaluation uses arm-specific thresholds
Findings apply to that cohort and to this threshold protocol
Gradient settings gave nearly identical outcomes

The one-step (FGSM-like) and five-step (BIM-like) gradient settings gave nearly identical round-5 outcomes, and identical label counts for every arm and seed, although their step rules differ. This is an observed result, and its cause was not tested
The two gradient settings should not be counted as separate evidence of robustness at this bound. A different or stronger gradient attack may give different results

A rerun from the downloaded data matched 5 of 15 original runs to within float32 rounding and 3 to within 3 × 10⁻⁵, and 7 showed small drift, up to 3.3 points in single round values. The original environment and exact code version are unknown

Tables 7 to 11 report the original outputs, whose five-seed means differ from the rerun by at most 0.46 points. The extension uses rerun outputs for seeds 17 to 21. Neither bit-for-bit reproduction nor the archived runner's identity with the original code is claimed
The partitions come from a third-party redistribution. The official test partition is identical in content, and the official training partition was not compared
The training partition's identity rests on the Zenodo checksum

Wall-clock time from one machine and a small NumPy model, excluding test-time evaluation. Each arm's time includes attack generation against its own model, which depends on the attack, so arm differences combine update and attack costs
Costs should not be extrapolated to larger detectors, and small differences are not read as policy costs
